title: Freezing Motion
summary: Spinning toys showed that quick pictures in a row can look like they are moving. Then faster photo plates let a photographer named Muybridge catch a galloping horse in mid-air with a row of cameras. His pictures proved that horses really fly, all four feet off the ground!

sections.heading: Toys That Fooled the Eye
paragraphs: Long before anyone could photograph motion, people were playing with toys that made motion out of nothing. They were sold in toy shops and opticians' shops in the 1820s and 1830s, and they turned living rooms into tiny laboratories of the human brain. Each one used the same surprising discovery: show the eye a series of slightly different pictures fast enough, and you will see something move that is really standing still.

The simplest was the thaumatrope, a name that roughly means 'wonder turner'. It was just a small cardboard disc with a picture on each side and a piece of string tied to the left and right edges. On one side you might see a bird, and on the other an empty cage. Twirl the strings between your fingers so the disc spins fast, and the bird appears to sit inside the cage. The first commercial sets went on sale in London in April 1825, sold by W. Phillips in boxes of 12 or 18 discs. The London doctor John Ayrton Paris is usually given credit for the toy, and he described it in a children's science book in 1827. But according to the mathematician Charles Babbage, the idea began with a friendly challenge: the astronomer John Herschel asked Babbage how he could see both sides of a coin at once, and the answer was to spin it on a table. A geologist friend, William Henry Fitton, then made a card version with a parrot on one side and a cage on the other.

The thaumatrope blended two pictures, but it could not tell a story. In December 1832, a Belgian physicist named Joseph Plateau came up with a toy that really animated a sequence. Almost at the same moment, an Austrian mathematician, Simon Stampfer, invented nearly the same thing in Vienna. Plateau's version became known as the phenakistiscope, from Greek words meaning something like 'deceiving viewer'. Plateau and Stampfer had both been inspired by experiments with spinning wheels by the English scientist Michael Faraday.

Here is how it worked. Around the edge of a cardboard disc were narrow slits. Between the slits and the centre was a ring of drawings, perhaps a juggler, a dancer or a pumping blacksmith, each one a little further through the movement than the last. You held the disc up to a mirror, with the pictures facing the glass, spun it, and peeked through the slits as they whirled past your eye. Each slit gave you a split-second glimpse of one drawing reflected in the mirror before the card blocked your view again. Glimpse, dark, glimpse, dark, and the drawings seemed to come alive and move smoothly round and round. Narrow slits made the pictures sharper, but darker.

Publishers in London, Paris, Vienna and elsewhere began selling sets of discs in 1833. There was only one problem: just one person at a time could peek through the slits. Still, the phenakistiscope was the first widely popular device to show a smooth illusion of motion, and every film and cartoon you have ever watched relies on the same idea of quick separate pictures.

sections.heading: Wheels of Life and Rings of Mirrors
paragraphs: In January 1834 a British mathematician, William George Horner, from Bristol, published a clever variation. Instead of a flat disc, he imagined a hollow drum with slits cut in its sides and pictures arranged on a strip inside. He called it the daedaleum, after Daedalus, the inventor of Greek myth. For some reason Horner's plans to sell it stalled, and for decades the idea mostly slept.

Then, in the 1860s, a Brown University student in America named William Ensign Lincoln improved the design so that the slits sat above the picture strip, and the strips could be swapped easily. The toy company Milton Bradley began selling it in 1866, and a US patent followed in April 1867. Lincoln gave it the name that stuck: zoetrope, from Greek words for 'life' and 'turning', a translation of its nickname, the 'wheel of life'. A whole family could gather round the spinning drum, each person looking through a different slit, and watch horses jumping, acrobats tumbling or a man endlessly being bitten by a dog. Paper strips could be bought by the dozen, so it was like owning a cinema with a very short programme.

The slits had a downside, though. They let in only a sliver of light, so the moving pictures looked dim, and they slightly squashed the image. In 1877 a French science teacher and inventor named Émile Reynaud solved this beautifully. In his praxinoscope (roughly 'action viewer'), the slits were gone. Instead, a ring of small flat mirrors stood around the centre of the drum, one mirror for each picture on the strip. As the drum turned, you looked at the mirrors, and each one showed you a picture at just the right instant. The images were brighter, clearer and less distorted than in a zoetrope.

Reynaud kept improving his idea. In 1879 he made a version hidden in a box with a little theatrical stage set, so the animated figure appeared to move in front of scenery. Around 1880 he showed a projecting version, which went on sale from 1882, and in 1888 he patented the Théâtre Optique, which projected long painted picture strips onto a screen for an audience. That story belongs to the history of animation. For now, notice what all these toys had in common: every picture was drawn by hand. Nobody yet knew exactly what a real horse or a real bird did in a fraction of a second, so artists could only guess.

sections.heading: Dry Plates: Photography Gets Faster
paragraphs: To photograph a real moving creature, photographers needed something the wet collodion plate could not give them: speed. A wet plate needed a few seconds of exposure in daylight, and it had to be prepared on the spot. Some tricks could make it work faster in very bright sun, but it was still awkward and messy.

The breakthrough came from an English doctor named Richard Leach Maddox. He was a keen photomicrographer, someone who takes photographs through a microscope, and he worked with wet plates constantly. The ether fumes from the collodion were making him unwell, so he went looking for a different substance to hold the silver crystals. He chose gelatin, the clear protein that makes jelly wobble, made by boiling animal skin and bones.

On 8 September 1871, the British Journal of Photography published his article, 'An Experiment with Gelatino-Bromide'. He described mixing silver nitrate and a bromide salt into warm gelatin so that tiny crystals of silver bromide formed inside it, then spreading this 'emulsion' onto glass and letting it dry. Maddox's own plates were slow and not very reliable, and he freely admitted that more work was needed. Like Archer, he did not patent the idea and gave it to the world.

Others quickly took up the challenge. The most important discovery came from Charles Harper Bennett in 1878: if the emulsion was kept warm for hours or days before coating, a process called ripening, the silver bromide crystals grew larger and much more sensitive. Suddenly, gelatin plates were not slower than wet plates but many times faster. Exposures could be shortened to a fraction of a second, short enough to be called 'instantaneous'. That speed also meant cameras needed a proper shutter, a fast-moving flap or blade, because simply taking off and replacing a lens cap by hand was now far too slow.

Just as important, the new plates were dry. They could be manufactured in a factory, packed in boxes, stored for months and developed whenever convenient, days or even weeks after exposure. By the late 1870s companies in Britain and the United States were selling ready-made dry plates. Photographers no longer had to haul a darkroom tent up a mountain or across a battlefield. They could simply take a box of plates and a camera, and leave the chemistry for later. One of the people who saw the business opportunity was a young man in New York State who would soon build a plate-coating machine. We will meet him at the end of this part.

sections.heading: A Photographer and a Railroad Millionaire
paragraphs: Our next hero was a man who kept reinventing himself, even his own name. He was born Edward James Muggeridge in 1830 in Kingston upon Thames, a town near London. As a young man he moved to America and worked as a bookseller in San Francisco. In 1860 he was badly hurt when a stagecoach crashed near the Texas border, and people who knew him later said his personality seemed changed afterwards. He went back to England to recover, learned photography, and returned to California calling himself Muybridge, a spelling he believed was closer to the old Anglo-Saxon form of his name. Later he even began spelling his first name Eadweard.

Muybridge became a celebrated landscape photographer. In 1867 he photographed Yosemite Valley, and his views of waterfalls and cliffs were sold widely, including as stereo cards. He photographed the coast, lighthouses, the new railroads and the city of San Francisco. His life also had a very dark chapter: in 1874 he shot and killed a man he believed was involved with his wife. At his trial in 1875 the jury acquitted him, finding the killing 'justifiable' under the ideas of that time, though historians today see the case as a troubling one.

The man who changed Muybridge's career was Leland Stanford, a former governor of California who had become enormously rich building the Central Pacific Railroad. Stanford owned a farm at Palo Alto, south of San Francisco, where he bred and trained racehorses, especially trotters, which pull a light two-wheeled cart called a sulky. Stanford was fascinated by the science of how horses move, because he wanted to train them to go faster.

There was a question that horse experts had argued about for a very long time. When a horse trots or gallops, is there ever a moment when all four of its hooves are off the ground at once? The legs move too fast for the human eye to be sure. Painters had their own answer: for centuries they had shown galloping horses in a 'flying gallop', with front legs stretched forward and back legs stretched behind, like a rocking horse. A popular story claims Stanford made a 25,000-dollar bet on the question, but that tale is a legend; historians have found no good evidence for it. What is clear is that Stanford wanted proof, and he hired Muybridge to get it.

Muybridge first tried in 1872 or 1873, photographing Stanford's famous trotter Occident with a single camera. The image was so blurry and underexposed that it showed little more than a smudged outline, and it was never properly published. Stanford's money, newer and faster plates and an ingenious plan would make the next attempt a world-famous success.

sections.heading: Twelve Cameras and a Flying Horse
paragraphs: By 1878, Muybridge had built an amazing outdoor laboratory beside the track at Stanford's farm. Along one side of the track stood a long shed holding a row of 12 large cameras, each pointing across the track. On the other side stood a tall white wall, marked with numbered vertical lines, so that the position of the horse's legs could be measured against them. The white background bounced back as much sunlight as possible, which helped with the very short exposures.

Each camera had a fast shutter, worked by springs or rubber bands, which could snap open and shut in a tiny fraction of a second. Muybridge then needed a way for the horse to press the shutters itself, one after another, exactly as it passed each camera. His answer was to stretch threads or wires across the track. For a trotter pulling a sulky, the metal wheel of the cart passed over the wires and completed an electric circuit, which fired the shutters with electromagnets. For a horse galloping with a rider, threads across the track were snapped by the horse's body as it ran. Either way, one camera after another fired in quick succession, like a ripple running down a line of dominoes.

On 15 June 1878, Muybridge staged a demonstration and invited newspaper reporters to watch. A horse thundered down the track, the wires and threads were tripped, and the 12 shutters clicked in a fraction of a second. Muybridge developed the plates on the spot, while the reporters waited. Within minutes, the witnesses could see a sequence of silhouettes, each one frozen at a different instant of a single stride. The most famous sequence from these June trials, usually dated 15 or 19 June, shows a mare called Sallie Gardner, ridden by a jockey listed as G. Domm.

Think about what this meant. No human being had ever been able to look at a galloping horse frozen in time. Now anyone could hold a card in their hands and study, frame by frame, what a horse's legs were really doing. Muybridge's photographs were published as a series of cards called The Horse in Motion, and drawings based on them soon appeared in magazines such as Scientific American.

The answer to the old question was yes: there is a moment when all four hooves leave the ground at once. But the photographs held a bigger surprise. The flying moment did not look anything like the famous paintings. The horse was not stretched out in a graceful leap with its legs pointing forwards and backwards. Instead, at the moment it was airborne, its legs were tucked up together underneath its belly, bunched like a coiled spring. The 'flying gallop' that artists had painted for centuries was simply wrong.

Many people refused to believe it at first. The poses looked clumsy, almost ugly, and some critics said the camera must be lying. But the same results came again and again, and soon painters began to change how they drew horses. Some artists studied Muybridge's photographs carefully to get anatomy right, while others complained that a frozen instant was not how the eye actually experiences motion. This debate, between what a camera records and what we perceive, has continued ever since.

Muybridge did not stop at one horse. In 1879 he expanded the setup to 24 cameras, and he photographed horses walking, trotting, galloping and jumping, as well as dogs, deer, oxen and people running and leaping. Fame soon followed. He travelled to Europe and gave lectures in Paris and in London, including at the Royal Institution in 1882. That same year, however, Stanford published a book called The Horse in Motion, written by his friend Dr J. D. B. Stillman, which used Muybridge's pictures but gave him hardly any credit. Muybridge was furious, and the two men fell out.

sections.heading: The Zoopraxiscope and Animal Locomotion
paragraphs: Muybridge wanted audiences to see his sequences move, not just study them frame by frame. So in 1879 he designed a projector he called the zoopraxiscope, and it was ready by early 1880. It was a kind of magic lantern, an older projector that shone a powerful light through a glass picture and a lens onto a screen, combined with the spinning disc of a phenakistiscope.

The pictures were painted around the edge of a glass disc about 16 inches (roughly 40 centimetres) across. They were based on his photographs, mostly as silhouettes painted by an artist whose name is not known. A slotted metal disc acted as a shutter, so the audience saw each picture only for an instant. Turn the handle, and on the screen a horse galloped, a man ran or a pair of dancers whirled around, larger than life. Because the images were stretched slightly by the spinning, the painted figures were drawn a little longer than in the photographs to make them look natural on the screen.

Muybridge used the zoopraxiscope in his lectures from 1880 to 1895, and audiences in America and Europe watched in amazement. It is often counted as one of the first machines to project moving pictures based on photographs, and it probably helped inspire later inventors, including Thomas Edison's team. The zoopraxiscope and most of its discs are still kept today at the Kingston Museum, in the English town where Muybridge was born.

His biggest project came next. From 1883 to 1886, with support from the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, Muybridge photographed movement on an enormous scale. Using the new, fast gelatin dry plates and banks of cameras, he recorded men and women walking, running, jumping, climbing stairs, carrying buckets and throwing balls, as well as horses, elephants, tigers, camels, birds and many other animals, some of them borrowed from the Philadelphia Zoo. People were usually photographed in front of a background grid, so their movements could be measured.

In 1887 he published the results as Animal Locomotion: 781 large plates containing around 20,000 separate photographs. Artists, doctors, scientists and engineers have used it ever since. It also changed art itself. Painters such as Marcel Duchamp, decades later, were inspired by the idea of a body broken up into a sequence of moments. Even today, animators study Muybridge's sequences to learn how a body really moves.

sections.heading: Marey's Photographic Gun
paragraphs: Across the Atlantic, a French scientist was chasing the same dream from a different direction. Étienne-Jules Marey was a physiologist, a scientist who studies how living bodies work. He started with the heart and blood, inventing instruments that drew wavy lines on paper to record a person's pulse. Then he turned to movement: how people walk, how horses trot and, most of all, how birds fly. When he saw Muybridge's horse photographs, he realised that photography could become a scientific measuring tool.

Muybridge's method used many cameras, each taking a picture from a slightly different spot. Marey wanted a single camera, with one viewpoint, that could take a rapid series of pictures in a row. In 1882 he built a remarkable device shaped like a rifle, called the chronophotographic gun ('chrono' means time). It had a wooden stock you held against your shoulder and a long barrel containing the lens. Instead of bullets, there was a round drum holding a light-sensitive plate.

When Marey aimed at a flying bird and pulled the trigger, clockwork turned the plate in steps, and a shutter flicked open for each step. The gun could take about 12 pictures every second, each with an exposure as short as about 1/700 of a second. He could follow a seagull or a pelican across the sky, just like a hunter aiming a shotgun, but instead of hurting the bird he brought home a circle of tiny photographs showing its wings rising and falling. Marey's idea was itself inspired by an earlier invention, the 'photographic revolver' that the astronomer Jules Janssen had built in 1874 to record the planet Venus passing in front of the Sun.

Marey soon moved on to even better methods. He built cameras that recorded many positions of a moving subject on a single fixed plate, so a runner dressed in black against a black background, with white stripes along the arms and legs, became a beautiful pattern of lines showing the whole motion at once. By about 1889 he was making cameras that used long strips of flexible film instead of glass. He studied falling cats, jumping athletes, swimming fish and the swirling smoke trails of air, which helped lead to early wind tunnels for studying flight.

Marey was not trying to make entertainment. He wanted to measure nature. But his single-camera series of pictures, taken rapidly through one lens onto a moving strip, is exactly what a movie camera does. His work helped scientists studying motion and inspired the inventors, in France and elsewhere, who soon built the first true motion-picture cameras.

sections.heading: A Light in a Rochester Kitchen
paragraphs: By 1888 the pieces of a revolution were lying on the table. Toys had shown that a series of quick pictures could fool the brain into seeing movement. Muybridge had shown that a camera could freeze a galloping horse. Marey had shown that a single camera could take a rapid series of pictures. And thanks to Maddox and Bennett, photographic plates were dry, fast and could be made in a factory. What was still missing was something flexible and cheap enough for ordinary people, and long enough to hold hundreds of pictures in a row.

Meanwhile, in Rochester, New York, a young bank clerk had been spending his evenings doing something unusual. After a full day of adding up numbers at the bank, he came home and experimented late into the night in his mother's kitchen, mixing gelatin emulsions and coating glass plates, sometimes falling asleep in his clothes. He had first bought a camera for a holiday trip and had been shocked by how heavy, messy and complicated photography was. He was convinced that it could be made simple enough for anyone. His name was George Eastman.

deepDive: Why do the toys in this part work? For much of the 1800s the standard answer was 'persistence of vision': the idea that an image lingers on the eye for a fraction of a second, so pictures blend together. Psychologists now think this explanation is too simple. Lingering images would produce blurry overlaps, not convincing motion. Instead, the brain actively interprets a series of slightly different, briefly flashed images as one object moving, an effect called apparent motion (studied by Max Wertheimer and others in the early 1900s). The slits in a phenakistiscope or zoetrope matter because they act as a shutter, cutting each picture into a short flash and preventing smearing. Muybridge's achievement also depended on chemistry and engineering. Ripened gelatin emulsions were dramatically more sensitive than wet collodion, and a bright white backdrop reflected as much light as possible, so even very short exposures (often quoted as around 1/1000 to 1/2000 of a second for his shutters, though exact figures are debated) could record a silhouette. The photographs are mainly outlines; fine detail was limited, and some published versions were retouched, a point that critics raised at the time. Historians also discuss credit. Muybridge's 1878 results were genuine and groundbreaking, but the electrical triggering system relied on engineers from Stanford's Central Pacific Railroad, and Stanford's 1882 book barely mentioned Muybridge, damaging his reputation in Britain for a time. Muybridge's sequences are not quite 'movies': each frame comes from a different camera at a slightly different viewpoint, and the intervals depend on the horse's speed rather than a steady clock. Marey's approach, with one lens and evenly timed exposures, is closer in principle to cinema, which is why many historians see the two men as complementary: Muybridge proved that instants could be captured, Marey showed how to record them systematically. Their work also launched biomechanics, the scientific study of movement, used today in sports science, medicine and robotics. Finally, the famous 25,000-dollar wager is a good example of how legends attach themselves to inventions; Stanford's interest in improving his racehorses is a much better documented motive.
funFact: Muybridge's zoopraxiscope and most of its painted glass discs are kept at the Kingston Museum in Kingston upon Thames, the English town where he was born and died.

check.q: What did Muybridge's 1878 photographs show about a galloping horse?
